protections: P1 (absent in the pin): every outbound translation URL is validated against an allowed destination before dispatch - reads built from loadPath (string, function or promise) plus interpolated lng/ns (lib/index.js:55-66) and writes built from addPath (lib/index.js:118-125).

P2 (absent in the pin): the validation binds to the request actually performed - the transport chosen at lib/request.js:162-170, an app-supplied request/alternateFetch (lib/index.js:12, lib/request.js:95) and the final redirect target.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: create() is dormant unless saveMissing is enabled and addPath is truthy (lib/index.js:112); it is an opt-in write endpoint the app configures, while the advisory is about loading translations.
loadPath/addPath is trusted app configuration and lng/ns are normally plain language and namespace codes, so checking the configured string or the raw language argument looks sufficient.
loadUrl is an internal chokepoint the backend calls itself; it appears in the public typings but is never documented in the README, so apps are not expected to call it with their own URL.
fetch is the modern default path; the XMLHttpRequest implementation is a legacy fallback exercised only by the polyfill test script, so a fetch-side check looks complete.
options.request and options.alternateFetch are application-supplied code - the app already owns the destination - so validating inside the default transport seems sufficient.
the configured load/add host is trusted and following redirects is normal HTTP; revalidating or refusing redirects would break CDN canonicalisation and is outside a URL-prefix check.

the visible values here are the legitimate ones - relative defaults, falsy abort, file:// in Node, query strings and a verbatim URL handed to custom request - so an absolute-http(s)-only rule looks like the safe reading of the advisory.

masking: T7 (redirect) only becomes reachable once an origin/host check exists on the constructed URL: a blocked URL is still reachable through a redirect served by an allowed origin.
T2 (create/addPath) is dormant unless saveMissing is enabled and addPath is truthy (lib/index.js:112; README.md:140).
T3's promise-valued loadPath branch only runs when the app passes a function returning a promise (lib/index.js:60; test/http.spec.js:197).

conflicts.what: A rule that requires an absolute http(s) URL before dispatch rejects the default relative loadPath (lib/index.js:6; README.md:134) and the relative path custom request handlers currently receive verbatim (test/http.spec.js:231, test/http.spec.js:252).
Holding addPath to the loadPath origin rejects the default relative addPath (lib/index.js:7; test/http.spec.js:263) and legitimate CDN-read plus own-API-write setups.
Resolving or normalising the URL for validation changes the string handed to options.request, which the tests assert exactly (test/http.spec.js:252, test/http.spec.js:263).
A scheme allowlist that drops non-http(s) URLs breaks the Node file:// loading path the XHR branch exists to serve (lib/request.js:162; CHANGELOG.md:100).

fairness_risks: Relative loadPath/addPath are the documented defaults (lib/index.js:6-7, README.md:134, README.md:142) and are passed unchanged to custom request handlers (test/http.spec.js:250-252, test/http.spec.js:262-263); a rule that refuses relative URLs or rewrites them breaks normal browser use.

The falsy-loadPath abort must still resolve with {} and no error (README.md:119; lib/index.js:63; test/http.spec.js:313), so a rule that rejects an empty or non-absolute URL breaks a documented feature.
file:// loading in Node is a legitimate non-http use (lib/request.js:162; CHANGELOG.md:100); a scheme allowlist must not refuse it.

queryStringParams are appended by the transport (lib/request.js:38-49, lib/request.js:122-123) and must keep working (test/request.spec.js:18-26), so a rule that rejects URLs carrying query strings is over-broad.
Multi-load joins languages and namespaces with '+' (lib/index.js:64; README.md:124) and language tags contain '-' (region/script); a charset rule on lng/ns must accept these shapes.

Function-valued and promise-valued loadPath must keep working (lib/index.js:56-63; test/http.spec.js:161-165, test/http.spec.js:189-222), so a rule that only accepts string loadPath options breaks supported configuration.

design.why: Four independent judgements on top of one shared read-side guard. T1 is the reported URL-validation route and is fast to find; T2 is the same request sink reached from create/addPath, which a load-path guard never touches, is dormant by default and has a strong reason to be dismissed (deepseek-type). T7 defeats any URL check through a redirect served by an allowed origin, protection never existed there and it reads as normal HTTP (deepseek-type). T8 forces the rule to stay origin/scheme-scoped rather than absolute-only so the relative defaults, falsy abort, file://, query strings and the custom-request contract keep working (mimo-type; over-hardening is the failure mode). T3/T4/T5/T6 are shape and placement variants of the same read-side guard and are kept in group one rather than counted as separate stack members. The remaining groups are the write dispatch (T2), the transport/redirect policy (T7) and the rule-shape constraint (T8).

unverified: The A fix (4cee84f229c6) and B fix (07e028862b25) are not present in the pinned checkout, and the worktree contains no validator at all (only url.indexOf('file:') at lib/request.js:162), so a_fix_leaves_b_open=true and b_in_code_a_wrote=false are inferred from the candidate metadata (link = previous patch, szz_status H3b2) rather than read from the fix diffs.
The GHSA/CVE texts were not available in the worktree; which route the B advisory names (loadPath read route versus addPath write route) is inferred from the code, not from the advisory wording.

Fetch follows redirects by default and XHR cannot restrict redirect targets; those are platform behaviours, not lines in this repository (the repo only omits any redirect option: lib/index.js:19-23, lib/request.js:89-94, lib/request.js:146-149).

Whether the hidden behavioural tests call loadUrl directly, install a custom request spy, enable saveMissing, or serve an HTTP redirect is unknown, so the relative weight of T2/T4/T6/T7 is not verified.

cross-fetch 4.1.0 is only a fallback fetch implementation (package.json:29-31, lib/request.js:28-36); no advisory fix appears to belong to a dependency upgrade, but no dependency changelog was inspected beyond package.json.
